Reviews · Persian poetry

Shahnameh

The Persian Book of Kings, Abolqasem Ferdowsi, translated by Dick Davis

4.2 of 5from 1,240 readers

Ferdowsi finished his poem around 1010, after thirty years: some fifty thousand couplets of the kings of Iran, from the first men to the Arab conquest, with Rostam and his horse Rakhsh at the heart of it. Two and a half centuries later the potters of Kashan were still writing its verses round the borders of the tiles they made for shrines and palaces.

Your review

Tell other readers what you made of it.

How was it?

Sohrab and Rostam undid me on a train. Davis keeps the prose moving and lets the verse rise where it should.

Parisa, March

Long, and the middle reigns blur together. The ending, with the last Sasanian king hiding in a mill, is worth the walk.

Tom, January

# lustre-stars A rating made of real Kashan lustre tiles. The picture is one photograph of five eight-pointed star tiles and the four cross tiles locked between them (13th–14th century, The Met). Each star is a radio button. Choose a value and a lamp held by someone standing to your left lights the tiles up to it. Their lustre, the metallic film fired onto the glaze, flashes gold and copper the way it does as you walk past a real wall. Tiles past the value stand in the shade. Nothing moves but the light. ```html
How was it?
``` The radios are real. Keep them in this order: input, then its label, five times. The CSS places each label over its own star, and the value posts with the form. Or call `lustreStars(root, options)` yourself. It returns `destroy()`, which also carries `hold(value, x)` (light the frieze as if that star were hovered, the lamp aimed at `x` in 0–1; `hold()` releases) and, on a read-only frieze, `set(value)`. ## In life / Here | In life | Here | |---|---| | Kashan potters (the Abu Tahir family among them) painted lustre over an opaque white or cobalt-and-turquoise glaze and fired it a second time in a smoky, reducing kiln, leaving a film of silver and copper particles well under a micron thick. | The tiles are photographs of real ones: five stars (41.165.20, .23, .18, .11, .13) and four crosses (.37, .32, .33, .39), The Met, cut from one photograph along their own joints. Nothing is drawn. | | Stars and crosses were set together in dados and on tomb walls (Imamzada Yahya at Varamin, 1262; the Ilkhan palace at Takht-i Sulaiman, 1270s). The crosses' arms fit between the stars' points. Each tile was set by hand, a degree or two off its neighbours. | The setting is the panel's own, photographed square-on. Each tile is given a small random tilt (σ ≈ 1.7°) and a rounded rim from its own outline, so no two tiles catch alike. | | No two tiles are alike: animals, trees, palmettes, interlace, with verses (often from the *Shahnameh*) or Qur'anic text round the border. | Five different stars: an arabesque, a dappled ass, an interlace, a flowering tree, a palmette. The inscription bands are as photographed. | | Lustre is dull brown in flat light and flashes metallic when a lamp or window reflects off it at the right angle: gold on olive and amber film, copper on red-brown, with a blue-violet sheen at the edge of the reflection. The bare glaze gives back a small white glint. | Per pixel, where the painter laid film (and how thick it looks) was baked offline. The shader reflects a lamp off each tile: the film in its own colour pushed toward metal, a faint blue-violet shoulder, and a white glint on bare glaze. The colours were set against The Met's own low-angle photographs of these tiles. | | A person with a lamp standing to the left lights the near tiles and not the far ones. | The chosen value is how far the lamp's light reaches. The edge falls between stars, across the cross between them, soft like a door jamb's shadow. Hover previews another value, and the lamp follows the pointer. | No transformation: the tiles are never "fired" or gilded on the page. The light only reaches them, or doesn't. ## Options | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-tiles` | `tiles` | `-tiles.png` | the baked data (same origin) | | `data-value` | `value` | — | read-only frieze: the value, 0–5, fractions allowed | | `data-lamp` | `lamp` | `1` | 0–2, the lamp's strength (the demo's small read-only friezes use `.55`) | | `data-distance` | `distance` | `1.6` | how far away you stand: `distance` × 1.2 frieze widths, at every size, so a phone's pools are a desktop's. Nearer = the lamp's reflection is a smaller pool that travels further across the tiles as you move | The options object wins over the attributes. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--ink` | `#141312` | the focus mark under a star | | `--ink-3` | `#8a857d` | the stated value (`.ls-say`) | | `--sans` | system | the stated value's font | Size it by its width: the frieze keeps the photograph's ratio (2400 × 766). Each star is 20% of the width, so keep the frieze at least 230 px wide where it is a control: 44 px targets at 220 px. The demo's form frieze is `max-width: 640px` and full column width on a phone (~354 px, stars ~72 px). ## How it works **Offline** (`tools/`, Python, not loaded by the page; `tools/bake.sh` reruns it). - **The cut.** Tiles vs wall from chroma and texture against the grey wall's own colour. Each star is fitted as an affine eight-pointed star (two squares), and each of its sixteen straight edges is snapped along its normal to where the glaze's bright rim drops into a neutral gap. A compact watershed on "neutral darkness" (the joints are grey shadow; the painting is coloured) then separates all fourteen tiles. Each kept region is clipped to its fitted shape. The crosses' edges that met the removed top row are snapped inward to their own rim. Checked at 1:1 on every joint. - **The shadow.** The wall's own darkening in the photograph, relative to a smooth fit of the lit wall. It is kept only where a kept tile could have cast it (the photograph's light is upper left), and filled where the brass hanging tabs had been. - **The data**, one lossless grayscale PNG, two images of the albedo's size (2400 × 766) stacked (0.81 MB): - top: height, 1/32 px a step: a rounded rim from each tile's own distance-to-edge (1 − e^(−d/9 px)) plus the glaze's relief, band-passed from the photograph (σ 2.2–10 px). The runtime takes its slope as the normal. - bottom: tile id in the high nibble (0 = wall, 1–5 the stars left to right, 6–9 the crosses); lustre density in the low nibble. - Each tile's hand-set tilt (σ 0.03) is nine numbers, `TILT` in the runtime. Density is how far a pixel sits below its own tile's bare glaze (each tile's 93rd-percentile lightness, since these glazes photograph warm), excluding the in-glaze cobalt and turquoise by hue. **Runtime** (`lustre-stars.js`, one fragment pass, WebGL 1). - At each size the photograph is resampled once to the canvas. The data is box-filtered on the CPU to the same size (height and film averaged, tile id by majority) and the normal taken from the height's slope there, so the relief never aliases into sparkle. - **Reach.** Each tile has a start along the value: star *k* at *k* − 1, each cross half a step before the star to its right. The light's edge sweeps across a tile as the value passes through it. The fraction is mapped by area (f + 0.1 sin 2πf), so 4.2 lights a fifth of the fifth star's face. The edge is soft over about 1% of the width: a jamb's shadow, not a fade. - **The lamp.** The eye stands 1.6 × 1.2 frieze widths out, drawn a quarter of the way toward the middle of the screen, so the sheen slides as the page scrolls. The lamp stands at the same distance, opposite the eye about the point it is aimed at, so its reflection pool falls there. Unpointed, it aims at the middle of what it reaches; hovering, at the pointer (clamped to the lit part). - **Materials.** - Film: a lobe on the half-vector of width² 0.0022, narrower than the tiles' spread of tilt, so some tiles catch and some don't. It reflects in the film's own colour pushed toward gold or copper. Add to that a faint broad sheen (width² 0.05) and a blue-violet shoulder (width² 0.012) where the film is thick. - Bare glaze: a white glint (width² 0.0007). - The lit tile is the photograph at 0.98–1.04; past the reach it is the photograph at half the exposure, and no lobe of any kind (they are multiplied by reach², so the penumbra never glints, whatever the tilt). Highlights roll off toward white instead of clipping. - **Springs.** The value and the lamp's aim each run on a critically damped spring (periods 0.42 s and 0.6 s) at a fixed 120 Hz step. - **Phone.** A tap checks the radio. Tilting the phone turns the wall under the lamp (up to 0.12 rad, via `tilt.js`), so different lit tiles catch; tiles past the value never do. ## Behaviour and cost - Draws only while something moves (the value or the lamp easing, a scroll, the tilt), and only on screen. Idle, nothing runs. - Assets: `frieze.webp` 0.61 MB, `frieze-tiles.png` 0.81 MB (downloaded once and cached; each frieze reads it). The data is box-filtered once per size (about 20–60 ms for a desktop-size frieze). - Canvas DPR is capped at 2 and never finer than the photograph. - One WebGL context per frieze. The demo has four. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - A `
` with a `` and five native radios. Tab enters the group, arrow keys change the value, and it posts with the form (`required` works). Each label's text ("3 of 5, good") is in the tree. - The `` states the value in words. - Focus shows as a short ink rule under the focused star, never as an outline or glow on the tile. - The value reads without the light: the stated value, the labels, and the radios themselves. In forced-colours mode the real radios and their text appear in a row under the picture. - Without JS, WebGL or the data: the photograph stays, and the stars past the choice stand in a quiet CSS shade cut to each star's own outline (`clip-path`, measured). - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: the value lands at once, with one still frame and the lamp aimed at the middle of its reach. Pointer and tilt don't move the light. - The images are `alt=""`, the canvas is `aria-hidden`. A read-only frieze is `role="img"` with an `aria-label`. - Print shows the photograph. ## Honest limits - The panel itself is a museum assembly (The Met, 1974). The tiles are 13th–14th-century Kashan, but this arrangement of these nine is the museum's, not a building's. The star-and-cross setting is right. - The tilts and the rim are modelled, not measured: these tiles were photographed once, square-on. Lustre density is read from colour, so a very dark cobalt can pass for thin film in places. - A fifth of a star's area is its left point and a little more (28% of its width), so a partial value wants the frieze at 280 px or wider to read. The read-only frieze at 150 px is small for the drawing. It works as a pattern of light, not as five pictures. ## Credits See `assets/credits.json` and `assets/PICK.md`. - Photograph DP231256: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, the 91.1.106 panel group, tiles from the H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1941 (41.165.11, .13, .18, .20, .23, .32, .33, .37, .39). CC0. - Lighting structure from `components/gold-ground` (per-pixel material baked offline, one fragment pass, drawing only while something moves); `tilt.js` from the same piece.

# lustre-stars: the pick

Contact sheets (scratch, `tools/engine/jobs/lustre-hunt/`):
- `sheet-met-41165.jpg`: every Met record in the 41.165 group (Havemeyer gift, 1941), primary views: 30 star,
  cross and half-star tiles, 20.3 cm each.
- `sheet-met-41165-all.jpg`: all 55 views of the ten colour-photographed tiles from that group, including their
  low-angle shots and the panel they are mounted in.
- `sheet-met-other0.jpg`: 34 other Met star and cross tiles (12th–15th century; Kashan, Sultanabad, Takht-i Sulaiman).
- `sheet-444459.jpg`: the ten views published with Met 444459 (accession 91.1.106): the assembled panel in two
  campaigns, the 1974 key, close-ups.
- `sheet-aic.jpg`: Art Institute of Chicago, seven Ilkhanid lustre tiles on one grey ground (incl. the
  Imamzada Yahya star and cross pair, 71231 and 71227).
- `sheet-panels.jpg`: nine assembled panels on Commons (Berlin's Imamzada Yahya field, the V&A, Doha, Walters),
  for the real setting: joints, gaps, how far tiles stand proud.

Also searched: Cleveland (`cc0=1`: four Ilkhanid tiles, only one star), Commons categories for Imamzadeh Yahya and
lustre tiles (mostly CC BY-SA gallery shots at an angle). `engine.py inspect` ran on `met-orig/`, `aic/` and
`commons/` (`inspect.txt`). The pick passes clean: 4000 px, "detail present at every scale; not an enlargement".

## The photograph: The Met DP231256, a panel of Kashan lustre stars and crosses

One modern photograph (4000 × 2211, CC0) of a panel The Met assembled in 1974 from fourteen tiles. It's square-on,
on a grey wall, in soft even light from the upper left, with each tile's own shadow falling down and to the right.
The Met's key (`tile panel key.JPG`, published with the same record) names every position. **The bottom row is
exactly the frieze the brief asks for: five eight-pointed stars, and between them, locked into their notches, four
crosses.**

| position | accession | Met id | the drawing |
|---|---|---|---|
| star 1 | 41.165.20 | 450436 | an eight-lobed arabesque, cobalt and turquoise under red-brown lustre |
| star 2 | 41.165.23 | 450439 | a dappled ass among flowering plants, cobalt on an olive lustre ground |
| star 3 | 41.165.18 | 450434 | an interlace of palmettes round a small eight-pointed centre, red lustre |
| star 4 | 41.165.11 | 450427 | a flowering tree in a vase, amber lustre, turquoise dabs |
| star 5 | 41.165.13 | 450429 | a great palmette in a vase, copper-red lustre |
| cross | 41.165.37 | 450453 | palmettes round a cobalt roundel, olive lustre |
| cross | 41.165.32 | 450448 | birds and a rosette, dark lustre ground |
| cross | 41.165.33 | 450449 | spotted hounds (or foxes) in a thicket |
| cross | 41.165.39 | 450455 | ogival trellis round a cobalt heart |

All are stonepaste, inglaze cobalt and turquoise, lustre over an opaque white glaze, 20.3 cm, 13th–14th century,
probably Kashan, H. O. Havemeyer Collection, CC0. Each star carries an inscription band round its edge.

**Why this one.**
- **One wall.** The five stars are five different hands' worth of drawing (an animal, a tree, a palmette, two
  geometric) yet came from one group and sit in one panel under one light, so they read as one wall. No other
  source gives that. The AIC set is just as consistent but has only four Ilkhanid lustre stars and one cross, each
  photographed alone. Assembling them would mean placing tiles in a setting no one photographed.
- **The setting is real.** The joints, the gaps, the way the crosses' arms seat between the stars' points, and the
  shadow are the photograph's own. No tile is moved; they are only cut out of the row above.
- **Reads small.** At 390 px each star is ~72 px. The ass, the vase and the palmette still read; the two geometric
  stars read as pattern, which is what they are.
- **Lustre reference from the same tiles.** The older campaign (`wb-41.165.*`) photographed these exact tiles at a
  grazing angle (`450429-5`, `450427-4`, `450448-4`). There the red-brown film deepens toward copper, olive film goes
  gold, and the glaze takes a silvery-blue sheen. The shader's colours were set against those.

### Why not the others

| source | what it has | why not |
|---|---|---|
| **Met DP231256 (444459 / 91.1.106 panel)** | the whole panel, modern, 4000 px, square-on, one light | **picked** |
| Met `wb-41.165.*` single views | the same tiles, ~1400 px each, colour | older snapshots, each a slightly different angle and exposure, tiles still in the mount with neighbours showing; kept as the lustre reference |
| Met `wb-91.1.106bb` | the same panel, 1956 px | lower resolution, older light |
| Met 41.165.21–31 b/w views | many more stars from the group | black-and-white archive prints |
| AIC 92287, 71231, 106111 + cross 71227 | sharp, 2300 px, one grey ground | only one cross; four stars from different buildings; no setting |
| Met 450438 (41.165.22) | a panel of small stars and crosses, 1260–70 | 2000 px, tiles too small to read at 72 px |
| Met 445276, 448196 | the deer and the octagon stars (this panel's top row) | the top row; a 2-row frieze reads as nine stars, not five |
| Commons panels (Berlin, V&A, Doha) | Imamzada Yahya in situ settings | CC BY-SA gallery photographs at an angle, glare; used only to learn the setting |
| Cleveland 1915.524, 1915.638 | one star, one square | not a set |

## The cut

The tiles were cut along their own joints, offline (`tools/`):
1. the wall vs. the tiles (chroma and texture against the grey wall's own colour);
2. each star fitted as an affine eight-pointed star (two squares), its sixteen straight edges snapped one by one
   to the joint (where the glaze's bright rim drops into a neutral gap);
3. a compact watershed over the whole panel on "neutral darkness" (joints are grey shadow; the painting is
   coloured), seeded from shrunken tile shapes;
4. each region clipped to its own fitted shape plus a few pixels; the crosses' edges that met the removed top
   row snapped inward to their own rim.

Checked by overlays at 1:1 on every cross top (`lustre-work/out/cross-tops.jpg`). The brass hanging tabs and the
biscuit fringes left with the cut. Where they had interrupted the wall's shadow, the shadow is filled from around
them.
